label: Blisters, bullae and erosions
q: Which blistering disease is this, and at what level does it split?
lead: Blistering disorders are separated by three questions: how deep is the split, is it grouped or scattered, and are the mucosae involved. Flaccid and mucosal points intraepidermal; tense and pruritic points subepidermal. Biopsy from the edge of a lesion less than 24 hours old, and always send a second specimen in Michel medium for direct immunofluorescence.

stop.l: Extensive detachment with mucosal erosions and skin pain
stop.a: SJS/TEN. Burns unit or ICU, stop the culprit drug, ophthalmology within hours. Calculate SCORTEN.

stop.l: Rapidly spreading tense bullae with fever and hypotension
stop.a: Consider necrotizing soft-tissue infection or bullous cellulitis with sepsis. Surgical review now — imaging must not delay exploration.

stop.l: Vesicles in a dermatomal distribution involving the nasociliary branch (tip of nose)
stop.a: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Hutchinson sign. Same-day ophthalmology and systemic antivirals.

stop.l: Disseminated vesicles in an immunosuppressed or atopic patient
stop.a: Disseminated zoster or eczema herpeticum. Admit for intravenous acyclovir. Eczema herpeticum is regularly mistaken for infected eczema and treated with antibiotics alone.

stop.l: Widespread flaccid blisters with painful oral erosions preventing eating
stop.a: Pemphigus vulgaris. Admit for fluid and nutritional support and start immunosuppression under specialist care. Untreated, this is a fatal disease.

stop.l: Neonate or young child with peeling and positive Nikolsky, mucosae spared
stop.a: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome. Anti-staphylococcal antibiotics. The mucosal sparing is what separates it from TEN.

stop.l: Blistering or erosions involving the eyes with conjunctival scarring
stop.a: Suspect mucous membrane (cicatricial) pemphigoid (or, if acute, SJS/TEN). Refer to ophthalmology urgently - ocular scarring is preventable but progressive once established.

stop.l: Blisters over bony prominences in someone found unconscious
stop.a: Coma blisters. The skin is the least of it - establish why they were unconscious (drug overdose, carbon monoxide, ketoacidosis, stroke) and check creatine kinase and renal function, because the same pressure causes myonecrosis and rhabdomyolysis.

dx.look: Superficial, flaccid, easily ruptured blisters that quickly become scaly, crusted (corn-flake) erosions in a seborrheic distribution - scalp, face, central chest and back; mucous membranes are spared and intact blisters are rarely seen because the split is high in the epidermis.
fr: Scaly, crusted corn-flake erosions rather than tense blisters
Seborrheic distribution - scalp, face, central chest and back
Mucous membranes spared
Superficial Nikolsky sign
Burning or pain rather than itch
dx.cf: Biopsy shows a subcorneal acantholytic split; direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular IgG in the upper epidermis and anti-desmoglein 1 antibodies confirm it.
dx.hp: A subcorneal or upper-epidermal acantholytic blister; direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular (chicken-wire) IgG in the superficial epidermis, and anti-desmoglein 1 ELISA confirms it.
dx.assoc: Antibodies target desmoglein 1 - the same antigen cleaved by staphylococcal exfoliative toxin - so mucosa is spared. Drug-induced (penicillamine, ACE inhibitors) and endemic (fogo selvagem) forms exist.
dx.mgmt: Often milder than pemphigus vulgaris - topical corticosteroids for limited disease; dapsone or hydroxychloroquine as steroid-sparing agents; systemic corticosteroids with rituximab for extensive disease.

dx.look: A chronic subepidermal blistering disease that predominantly affects mucous membranes - oral (desquamative gingivitis), ocular (symblepharon), nasal, pharyngeal and genital - and heals with scarring; cutaneous involvement is limited, and ocular disease can progress to blindness.
fr: Erosions and scarring of oral, ocular or genital mucosa
Desquamative gingivitis
Ocular symblepharon or conjunctival scarring
Scarring at sites of healing
Older adults
ag: Widespread cutaneous blisters with little mucosal disease
dx.cf: Perilesional biopsy for histology and direct immunofluorescence (linear IgG/C3, often IgA, at the basement membrane); refer any eye involvement to ophthalmology urgently - scarring is preventable.
dx.hp: A subepidermal blister with a mixed dermal infiltrate and dermal scarring; direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG, C3 and often IgA along the basement membrane.
dx.assoc: Ocular involvement threatens sight - refer to ophthalmology urgently; the anti-laminin-332 subtype carries an increased malignancy risk and warrants an age-appropriate cancer screen.
dx.mgmt: Dapsone for mild disease; systemic corticosteroids with cyclophosphamide or rituximab for severe ocular or laryngeal disease; multidisciplinary care with ophthalmology, ENT and dentistry.

dx.look: Elderly patient. Tense bullae on normal or erythematous skin, with urticarial plaques and papules often preceding the blisters by weeks to months. Intensely pruritic. Flexural forearms, axillae, medial thighs, groin, lower legs. Mouth involved in only 10–35% and mildly.
fr: Age over 65
Tense blisters that do not rupture easily
Severe pruritus
Prodromal urticarial or eczematous phase
Mucosae spared or only mildly involved
Peripheral eosinophilia
ag: Flaccid blisters that rupture on touch
Severe painful mouth erosions dominating the picture
dx.cf: Perilesional biopsy for direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone. Serum indirect IF or BP180/BP230 ELISA supports it.
dx.hp: A subepidermal blister with an eosinophil-rich infiltrate; direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane, and on salt-split skin the deposits sit on the blister roof.
dx.assoc: Elderly patients; associated with neurologic disease (dementia, stroke, Parkinson) and occasionally drugs (gliptins, PD-1 inhibitors, loop diuretics). Serum BP180/BP230 ELISA supports the diagnosis.
dx.mgmt: A potent topical corticosteroid (clobetasol) is first-line and as effective as oral steroids for many; systemic prednisone with a steroid-sparing agent (doxycycline, methotrexate, azathioprine) for extensive disease.

dx.look: Usually begins in the mouth, and months may pass before skin lesions appear. Flaccid, easily ruptured blisters on normal skin leaving painful erosions and crusts. Nikolsky positive. Burning and pain rather than itch. Scalp, face, chest, axillae, groin, umbilicus.
fr: Painful oral erosions preceding skin disease
Flaccid blisters, mostly seen as erosions
Nikolsky sign positive
Burning pain rather than pruritus
Weight loss from inability to eat
dx.cf: Perilesional direct IF shows intercellular IgG and C3 in a net-like epidermal pattern. Desmoglein 3 ELISA for mucosal disease; desmoglein 1 and 3 for mucocutaneous.
dx.hp: Suprabasal acantholysis with a row-of-tombstones basal layer; direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular (chicken-wire) IgG, and anti-desmoglein 1/3 ELISA confirms and monitors.
dx.assoc: Mucosal erosions usually precede skin lesions; screen for the paraneoplastic variant (anti-envoplakin, an underlying lymphoproliferative disorder) when atypical or refractory.
dx.mgmt: Systemic corticosteroids with rituximab, now first-line for moderate-to-severe disease (steroid-sparing and disease-modifying); azathioprine or mycophenolate as alternatives.
dx.pat: Oral first, then seborrheic and flexural

dx.look: Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, preceded by tingling or burning, recurring at the same site. Rapidly become erosions with a scalloped border. Perioral or anogenital most often. In atopic dermatitis, dissemination gives eczema herpeticum with monomorphic punched-out erosions.
fr: Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base
Recurs at the same anatomical site
Prodromal tingling or burning
Scalloped erosion borders where vesicles have coalesced
Punched-out monomorphic erosions in an atopic patient
ag: No prior episodes and no prodrome
Strictly dermatomal with pain in one nerve distribution
Widespread tense bullae in an elderly patient
dx.cf: PCR from a deroofed vesicle base is the test of choice. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells within minutes but cannot separate HSV from VZV. Direct fluorescent antibody distinguishes them.
dx.hp: Ballooning degeneration with multinucleated giant keratinocytes, nuclear molding and steel-gray nuclear inclusions; histologically identical to varicella.
dx.assoc: Confirm with PCR (most sensitive), viral culture or a Tzanck smear; eczema herpeticum is a risk in atopic dermatitis and demands prompt systemic therapy.
dx.mgmt: Oral acyclovir, valacyclovir or famciclovir; intravenous acyclovir for disseminated disease or eczema herpeticum; suppressive therapy for frequent recurrences.
dx.pat: Perioral and anogenital, recurs same site

dx.look: Unilateral, dermatomal, does not cross the midline. Pain often precedes the rash by days. Grouped vesicles evolving to pustules and crusts over 7–10 days on an erythematous base. Thoracic and ophthalmic divisions most common.
fr: Strictly unilateral and dermatomal
Pain preceding the eruption by days
Does not cross the midline
Vesicles at differing stages within one dermatome
Age over 50 or immunosuppressed
ag: Recurrent at the same site (favors HSV)
dx.cf: PCR from vesicle fluid. Direct fluorescent antibody has a higher yield than culture. If more than 20 lesions lie outside the primary dermatome, treat as disseminated and screen for immunosuppression.
dx.hp: As for herpes simplex - ballooning degeneration with multinucleate giant cells; PCR distinguishes VZV from HSV.
dx.assoc: Dermatomal; ophthalmic (V1) involvement threatens sight (get ophthalmology) and disseminated zoster suggests immunosuppression. Postherpetic neuralgia is the main sequela.
dx.mgmt: Start an antiviral (valacyclovir or famciclovir) within 72 hours; provide analgesia; offer the recombinant zoster vaccine after recovery for prevention.

dx.look: Ferociously pruritic grouped papules and vesicles that the patient has almost always excoriated before you see them — so you find excoriations, not blisters. Symmetric on elbows, knees, buttocks, sacrum and scapulae. Associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy.
fr: Intractable itch and burning, worse than the visible signs
Excoriations at elbows, knees, buttocks, sacrum
Strictly symmetric
Personal or family history of celiac disease or thyroid disease
Rapid response to dapsone
ag: Intact tense bullae on the trunk
dx.cf: Direct IF of normal-appearing perilesional skin shows granular IgA in the dermal papillae — this is the diagnostic test. Serum tissue transglutaminase and endomysial antibodies support it.
dx.hp: A subepidermal vesicle with neutrophilic papillary microabscesses; direct immunofluorescence shows granular IgA in the dermal papillae - the specific finding.
dx.assoc: Gluten-sensitive enteropathy (usually silent) - check IgA anti-tissue-transglutaminase and anti-endomysial antibodies; there is an increased risk of thyroid disease and small-bowel lymphoma.
dx.mgmt: Dapsone gives dramatic relief (check G6PD first) plus a lifelong gluten-free diet, which lowers the dapsone requirement and the lymphoma risk.

dx.look: Annular or grouped papules, vesicles and bullae, classically arranged around the edge of an annular lesion — the string of pearls or cluster of jewels sign, especially in children. Oral erosions and conjunctival involvement occur. Vancomycin is the commonest drug trigger.
fr: Annular lesions with vesicles at the periphery
Cluster of jewels arrangement
Recent vancomycin
Child with perineal and perioral involvement
ag: Granular rather than linear IgA on immunofluorescence
dx.cf: Direct IF shows linear IgA along the basement membrane zone — that finding defines the disease and separates it from bullous pemphigoid and dermatitis herpetiformis.
dx.hp: A subepidermal blister with neutrophilic papillary microabscesses; direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgA along the basement membrane - the defining feature.
dx.assoc: Idiopathic or drug-induced (vancomycin is classic); in children it is chronic bullous disease of childhood with a string-of-pearls arrangement of blisters.
dx.mgmt: Stop any culprit drug; dapsone first-line (check G6PD), with topical or systemic corticosteroids as needed.

dx.look: Children most often. Flaccid superficial bullae that rupture leaving a shallow erosion with a collarette of scale and a golden-yellow crust. Staphylococcus aureus exfoliative toxin. No systemic upset unless it generalizes to SSSS.
fr: Child, warm humid conditions
Golden-yellow crust with a collarette
Superficial, heals without scarring
Contacts affected
dx.cf: Swab for culture and sensitivity — do this before treating, because MRSA changes the antibiotic choice. Gram stain shows clusters of cocci.
dx.hp: A subcorneal split with acantholysis and neutrophils; Gram stain shows cocci, as staphylococcal exfoliative toxin cleaves desmoglein 1.
dx.assoc: Staphylococcus aureus - swab for culture and MRSA. Widespread toxin effect in neonates and infants is staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.
dx.mgmt: Topical mupirocin for limited disease; an oral antistaphylococcal antibiotic (cephalexin, or clindamycin/doxycycline if MRSA) when extensive.

dx.look: One or a few sharply demarcated, round, dusky violaceous plaques that blister centrally, recurring at exactly the same site every time the drug is taken. Lips, genitals, hands. Heals with dense post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.
fr: Recurs at precisely the same site with each exposure
Sharply circumscribed round dusky plaque
Residual slate-gray hyperpigmentation between episodes
Few lesions, not generalized
NSAID, sulfonamide, tetracycline, paracetamol
dx.cf: Clinical, supported by the history of recurrence at a fixed site. Biopsy shows interface change with pigment incontinence. Generalized bullous fixed drug eruption can mimic TEN and is separated by the history and the absence of severe mucosal disease.
dx.hp: Interface dermatitis with numerous necrotic keratinocytes, basal vacuolization and pigment incontinence - a lichenoid, dyspigmenting pattern.
dx.assoc: Recurs at the same sites within hours of the culprit drug (NSAIDs, sulfonamides, tetracyclines); a generalized bullous form can mimic SJS/TEN and is potentially severe.
dx.mgmt: Identify and permanently avoid the drug; topical corticosteroids for localized disease; manage the generalized bullous form as a severe cutaneous drug reaction.
dx.pat: Recurs at the same fixed site

dx.look: Skin fragility and tense blisters on sun-exposed, trauma-prone sites — dorsal hands, forearms, face. Heals with milia and scarring. Hypertrichosis over the malar cheeks and sclerodermoid change. Associated with hepatitis C, alcohol, estrogen and iron overload.
fr: Blisters only on dorsal hands and other trauma-exposed sun-exposed sites
Milia within healing erosions
Skin fragility — minor knocks cause erosions
Malar hypertrichosis
Hepatitis C, alcohol excess, estrogen use
dx.cf: Urine porphyrins with a plasma porphyrin fluorescence scan. Urine shows pink-red fluorescence under a Wood lamp, intensified by dilute hydrochloric acid. Screen for hepatitis C, HIV, iron studies and liver function.
dx.hp: A subepidermal blister with festooning of the dermal papillae and PAS-positive thickened vessel walls; caterpillar bodies may be seen.
dx.assoc: Photosensitive blisters, skin fragility, milia and hypertrichosis on the dorsal hands; check hepatitis C, HIV, iron and HFE, alcohol and estrogen use. Confirm with elevated urinary uroporphyrins (urine fluoresces coral-pink under Wood lamp).
dx.mgmt: Remove triggers (alcohol, estrogen, iron) with sun protection, and use scheduled phlebotomy or low-dose hydroxychloroquine; treat any coexisting hepatitis C.

dx.look: Classic mechanobullous form: non-inflammatory tense blisters at trauma sites — knuckles, elbows, knees, sacrum, toes — healing with scars and milia. An inflammatory form closely mimics bullous pemphigoid and is separated only on immunofluorescence.
fr: Blisters at trauma-prone sites
Healing with scarring and milia
Skin fragility
Poor response to systemic steroids
dx.cf: Salt-split skin direct IF localizes IgG to the dermal (floor) side, which separates it from bullous pemphigoid where the deposit is on the epidermal (roof) side. Antibodies to type VII collagen by ELISA or Western blot.
dx.hp: A subepidermal blister; direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG at the basement membrane localizing to the blister floor (dermal side) on salt-split skin - separating it from bullous pemphigoid.
dx.assoc: Autoantibodies to type VII collagen; the mechanobullous form gives trauma-induced blisters, scarring and milia on acral sites, and it may accompany inflammatory bowel disease.
dx.mgmt: Often refractory - wound care and trauma avoidance; colchicine, dapsone or corticosteroids, and rituximab or IVIG for resistant disease.

dx.n: Acute bullous allergic contact dermatitis (poison ivy and other plants)
dx.look: Streaky, linear vesicles and tense bullae on well-demarcated erythematous, edematous plaques exactly where the plant brushed the skin - exposed forearms, legs or face - appearing within 12 hours to 3 days of re-exposure in a sensitized person. Ferociously itchy. Palms and soles are spared because the resin cannot penetrate thick stratum corneum.
fr: Linear or streaky arrangement of vesicles and bullae
Sharply confined to exposed skin that made contact, with spread at the periphery
Intense itch, often felt before anything is visible
Gardening, clearing brush or walking through woodland in the preceding days
Marked periorbital or facial edema when the face is involved
Palms and soles spared
ag: Blisters at trauma sites healing with milia and scarring
dx.cf: History and distribution. Patch testing identifies the allergen in non-plant cases; patch testing to urushiol itself is not done because it sensitizes. Blister fluid contains no allergen and cannot spread the rash - say so out loud, because everyone believes the opposite.
dx.hp: Marked spongiosis with intraepidermal vesiculation, exocytosis of lymphocytes and eosinophils, and papillary dermal edema; immunofluorescence is negative.
dx.assoc: Toxicodendron species (poison ivy, oak, sumac) and cross-reacting plants - mango rind, cashew shell oil, ginkgo, Japanese lacquer. Sensitization is lifelong, and oleoresin persists on clothing, tools and pet fur to re-expose. Ingested urushiol produces a systemic contact dermatitis.
dx.mgmt: Wash skin, clothing and contaminated tools with soap and water. Potent topical corticosteroids and cool compresses for limited disease; for extensive or facial involvement, prednisone tapered over 2 to 3 weeks - a shorter course reliably produces rebound.

dx.look: One or a few tense, clear-fluid blisters exactly where a force acted: over the heel or the ball of the foot after new shoes or a long walk, over a bony pressure point in someone found unconscious, or on tensely edematous legs and hands during acute fluid overload. No inflammation elsewhere, and no new lesions once the cause is removed.
fr: Blisters restricted to a pressure, friction or dependent site
A clear mechanical explanation - new footwear, a long march, manual work, prolonged immobility, sudden edema
Blisters over bony prominences with surrounding dusky erythema after a period of unconsciousness
Clear fluid rather than hemorrhagic or purulent
No new blisters once the cause is removed
ag: Crops of new blisters at untraumatized sites
dx.cf: History and site. A coma blister demands the question of why the person was unconscious - drug overdose, carbon monoxide poisoning, ketoacidosis or a neurologic event. If blisters keep appearing at untraumatized sites this is the wrong diagnosis: biopsy and send perilesional skin for direct immunofluorescence.
dx.hp: An intraepidermal or subepidermal split with a sparse or absent infiltrate; coma blisters characteristically show necrosis of eccrine sweat glands. Immunofluorescence is negative.
dx.assoc: Coma blisters point to drug overdose, carbon monoxide poisoning or another cause of prolonged immobility, and the same pressure can cause myonecrosis - check creatine kinase and renal function. Edema blisters follow rapid fluid overload in cardiac, renal or hepatic failure.
dx.mgmt: Remove the cause: footwear, pressure, fluid overload. Leave the roof on as a biological dressing, drain a tense blister at its edge with a sterile needle, dress non-adherently, and treat the underlying problem. Antibiotics only for genuine secondary infection.

dx.look: Bilateral, symmetric target lesions on the dorsal hands, palms, forearms, elbows and knees whose dull red centers blister, together with erosions and fibrin membranes on the lips and oral mucosa. Follows a herpes simplex outbreak by several days, or Mycoplasma infection in a child or young adult.
fr: Three-zone target lesions with a blistering or dusky center
Acral and symmetric - dorsal hands, palms, forearms, elbows, knees
Cold sore or genital herpes several days before onset
Crusted hemorrhagic cheilitis with oral erosions
Recurrent episodes over years
ag: Truncal dusky macules with skin pain and detachment over 10% of the surface
Tense blisters on urticarial plaques in an elderly patient
dx.cf: Clinical. Biopsy shows interface dermatitis with keratinocyte apoptosis and a subepidermal split, and direct immunofluorescence is negative - useful, because it excludes the autoimmune blistering diseases from the same specimen. The critical separation is from SJS.
dx.hp: Perivascular mononuclear infiltrate with upper dermal edema, apoptotic keratinocytes, focal epidermal necrosis and a subepidermal blister; severe cases show complete epidermal necrosis. Direct immunofluorescence is negative.
dx.assoc: Herpes simplex is the usual trigger and Mycoplasma pneumoniae the other; drug-triggered cases behave as EM major with prominent mucosal disease. Conjunctivitis can progress to keratitis and corneal ulceration, so involve ophthalmology when the eyes are affected.
dx.mgmt: Antiviral therapy for HSV-associated disease with continuous suppression to prevent recurrence, and a macrolide for Mycoplasma. Topical corticosteroids and analgesic mouthwash; admit EM major for fluids, mucosal care and ophthalmology review.

dx.look: Intensely pruritic urticarial papules and plaques starting on the abdomen, characteristically around the umbilicus, in the fourth to seventh month of pregnancy or immediately postpartum, evolving into tense vesicles and bullae. Mucous membranes are spared.
fr: Onset in the second or third trimester, or immediately postpartum
Begins on the abdomen, characteristically periumbilical
Urticarial plaques that go on to form tense vesicles and bullae
Ferocious pruritus
Flared by estrogen or progesterone-containing medication
Began earlier and more severely in a subsequent pregnancy
ag: Onset outside pregnancy or the postpartum period
Lesions confined to abdominal striae with periumbilical sparing
dx.cf: Perilesional direct immunofluorescence shows linear C3 along the basement membrane zone, with IgG in about 30%. BP180 ELISA is positive in over 70%, while indirect immunofluorescence detects antibody in only about 20% - so a negative serum study means nothing.
dx.hp: Subepidermal blister with papillary dermal edema and a perivascular lymphocytic and eosinophilic infiltrate; direct immunofluorescence shows linear C3, with IgG in a minority.
dx.assoc: Complement-fixing IgG1 antibodies to BP180 that bind amniotic epithelial basement membrane. There is a slight excess of premature and small-for-gestational-age births, so arrange obstetric surveillance; about 5% of neonates have transient urticarial or bullous lesions. It recurs earlier and more severely in later pregnancies and can flare with the combined oral contraceptive.
dx.mgmt: Potent topical corticosteroids with antihistamines for mild disease; prednisone 20 to 40 mg daily for blistering disease, tapered gradually after delivery. Coordinate with obstetrics.

dx.look: Blistering from birth or early childhood at sites of friction and trauma - hands, feet, elbows, knees - reproducibly provoked by rubbing and worse in hot weather. Simplex forms heal without scarring; dystrophic forms heal with atrophic scars, milia, nail loss and, in severe recessive disease, mitten-like fusion of the digits.
fr: Blistering since birth or infancy at the same trauma-prone sites
Family history of the same problem
Worse with heat, friction and exercise
Nail dystrophy or loss with dental enamel defects
Scarring, milia and pseudosyndactyly in dystrophic forms
Thick-walled blisters on the soles after marching or manual work in localized simplex disease
ag: First blistering episode in an older adult
dx.cf: Biopsy establishes the level of cleavage, defined further by immunofluorescence antigen mapping or electron microscopy, then genetic testing identifies the mutated gene. In an adult presenting for the first time, send direct immunofluorescence as well - epidermolysis bullosa acquisita is clinically identical and is treatable.
dx.hp: A non-inflammatory cleavage plane whose level defines the type: intraepidermal in simplex, through the lamina lucida in junctional, and below the lamina densa with scarring and milia in dystrophic disease. Immunoreactants are absent.
dx.assoc: Keratin 5 and 14 mutations in simplex disease, laminin and collagen XVII in junctional, and type VII collagen in dystrophic. Severe recessive dystrophic disease brings esophageal strictures, anemia, growth failure and aggressive squamous cell carcinoma arising in chronic erosions, so lifelong surveillance is required.
dx.mgmt: No curative therapy yet. Protective wound care with non-adherent dressings, a cool environment, soft ventilated footwear, nutritional support and infection control; severe junctional and dystrophic disease is managed as for burns, with multidisciplinary and DEBRA support.
dx.pat: Friction and trauma sites from birth

dx.look: Abrupt crops of tense vesicles and bullae on normal or erythematous skin, favoring sun-exposed skin, the upper trunk, neck and face, in a young adult with known or newly declaring systemic lupus. Little or no itch, healing without scarring, and a striking response to dapsone within days.
fr: Known systemic lupus, or serology and organ involvement that establish it
Abrupt crops of tense blisters on the upper trunk, neck, face and sun-exposed skin
Little or no pruritus
Heals without scarring or milia
Dramatic response to dapsone within 48 to 72 hours
Young adult, more often female and of African descent
ag: Elderly with an urticarial prodrome and severe itch
Blisters confined to trauma sites healing with milia
Painful oral erosions dominating the picture
dx.cf: Biopsy shows a subepidermal blister with neutrophilic papillary microabscesses that mimics dermatitis herpetiformis; direct immunofluorescence shows IgG with IgA and C3 at the basement membrane, localizing to the dermal side on salt-split skin. Antibodies to type VII collagen with a positive ANA and anti-dsDNA complete it - then assess the kidneys.
dx.hp: Subepidermal blister with a neutrophil-rich papillary infiltrate and leukocytoclasia; direct immunofluorescence shows IgG, often with IgA and IgM, plus C3 at the basement membrane zone, on the dermal floor of salt-split skin.
dx.assoc: An expression of active systemic lupus - check ANA, anti-dsDNA, complement, blood count, creatinine and urinalysis, because lupus nephritis frequently accompanies it.
dx.mgmt: Dapsone first-line, with a response within days (check G6PD first). Treat the underlying lupus with hydroxychloroquine plus corticosteroids and immunosuppression as the systemic disease requires.

ctx.s: Bullous pemphigoid is a disease of the elderly, Fitzpatrick 8e §6
Eczema herpeticum complicates atopic dermatitis, Fitzpatrick 8e §27

ctx.l: New drug in the last 8 weeks

ctx.s: Vancomycin is the commonest drug trigger for linear IgA disease

ctx.l: Hepatitis C, alcohol excess, or estrogen therapy
Known celiac disease or gluten sensitivity
ctx.s: Dermatitis herpetiformis is the skin expression of gluten-sensitive enteropathy, Fitzpatrick 8e §6

ctx.l: Currently pregnant or within 3 months of delivery
ctx.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §6 - pemphigoid gestationis begins in the fourth to seventh month or postpartum

ctx.l: Outdoor plant, garden or occupational contact in the last week
ctx.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §2 - allergic phytodermatitis follows Toxicodendron exposure

find.l: Blisters are tense and do not rupture easily
find.s: Subepidermal split gives a tense blister, Fitzpatrick 8e §6

find.l: Blisters are flaccid, or you find only erosions
find.s: Intraepidermal split gives a flaccid blister, Fitzpatrick 8e §6

find.l: Nikolsky sign positive
find.s: Nikolsky is positive in acantholytic disorders, Fitzpatrick 8e Introduction

find.l: Painful oral erosions, dominating the picture
find.s: PV almost always involves the mouth; BP does so in only 10–35%, Fitzpatrick 8e Table 6-3

find.l: Intense pruritus
Urticarial or eczematous plaques preceded the blisters
find.s: The prodromal urticarial phase of bullous pemphigoid, Fitzpatrick 8e §6

find.l: Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base
Strictly unilateral and confined to one dermatome
find.s: Dermatomal distribution is near-specific for zoster, Fitzpatrick 8e §27

find.l: Recurs at exactly the same site
find.s: Fixed recurrence distinguishes HSV and fixed drug eruption, Fitzpatrick 8e §27,§23

find.l: Pain preceded the rash by days
Symmetric on elbows, knees, buttocks and sacrum
find.s: The predilection sites of dermatitis herpetiformis, Fitzpatrick 8e Table 6-3

find.l: Excoriations rather than intact blisters
Annular lesions with vesicles at the periphery (cluster of jewels)
Golden-yellow crust with a peripheral collarette
Confined to dorsal hands and other sun-exposed trauma sites
Milia forming within healing erosions
find.s: Milia and scarring indicate a deep, sub-lamina densa split, Fitzpatrick 8e §6,§10

find.l: Skin fragility — minor trauma produces erosions
A single or few round dusky plaques with residual gray pigment
Peripheral eosinophilia
find.s: Eosinophilia occurs in bullous pemphigoid but not always, Fitzpatrick 8e §6

find.l: Superficial scaly-crusted erosions in a seborrheic distribution, mucosa spared
Erosions and scarring of ocular, oral or genital mucosa
Linear or streaky vesicles and bullae on an edematous plaque
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §2 - linear lesions of allergic phytodermatitis

find.l: Sharply confined to exposed skin that touched a plant or chemical
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §2 - eruption is confined to the site of exposure

find.l: One or a few blisters exactly at a pressure, friction or dependent site
Blisters over bony prominences after a period of unconsciousness
find.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin - coma blisters with eccrine gland necrosis

find.l: No new blisters appear once the cause is removed
Three-zone target lesions with a blistering center on the hands and forearms
Crusted hemorrhagic cheilitis with oral erosions after a cold sore
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §14 - erosive cheilitis of erythema multiforme major

find.l: Urticarial plaques and blisters beginning around the umbilicus in pregnancy
Onset in the second or third trimester or immediately postpartum
find.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §6 - onset from the fourth to the seventh month or postpartum

find.l: Blistering since birth or infancy at trauma-prone sites
Family history of the same blistering problem
Nail dystrophy or loss with dental enamel defects
Abrupt crops of tense blisters on sun-exposed skin in a young adult with lupus
Blistering cleared within days of starting dapsone
find.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin - rapid dapsone response in the neutrophil-rich subepidermal blistering diseases

find.l: Chronic red eye with conjunctival scarring, symblepharon or inturned lashes
find.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin - scarring conjunctivitis is the sight-threatening hallmark of mucous membrane pemphigoid

find.l: Lesions concentrated on the face, scalp and upper chest and clearly worsened by sun exposure
find.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin - the seborrheic and photoaggravated distribution of pemphigus foliaceus

test.l: Perilesional biopsy with direct immunofluorescence and anti-desmoglein 1 ELISA
test.w: Scaly, crusted erosions in a seborrheic distribution without mucosal disease.
test.p: Subcorneal acantholysis with intercellular IgG in the superficial epidermis and anti-Dsg1 antibodies confirms pemphigus foliaceus.
test.n: A negative direct immunofluorescence on a crusted lesion may reflect sampling - take perilesional skin and repeat if the picture fits.
test.x: Sample perilesional skin, not the crust; the superficial split is easily lost in a crusted or over-sampled specimen.

test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §6 Table 6-3 — linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane zone
test.w: Every suspected autoimmune blistering disease. This is the single test that separates the whole group, and it is the one most often omitted or taken from the wrong site.
test.p: Linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone confirms pemphigoid. Intercellular net-like IgG confirms pemphigus. Granular IgA in dermal papillae confirms dermatitis herpetiformis. Linear IgA confirms linear IgA disease.
test.n: A negative direct IF from correctly sampled perilesional skin makes an autoimmune blistering disease unlikely. From the wrong site it means nothing.
test.x: Take it from normal-appearing skin within 1 cm of a lesion, never from the blister itself — the immunoreactants are destroyed inside the blister. Send in Michel medium or fresh on saline gauze, not formalin. For dermatitis herpetiformis, sample uninvolved skin away from the lesion.

test.l: Lesional biopsy for routine histology (edge of a blister <24 h old)
test.w: Alongside direct IF, to establish the level of the split.
test.p: Suprabasal acantholysis confirms pemphigus vulgaris; acantholysis in the granular layer confirms pemphigus foliaceus; a subepidermal split with eosinophils suggests bullous pemphigoid; papillary microabscesses suggest dermatitis herpetiformis.
test.n: An old, ruptured or re-epithelializing blister gives uninterpretable histology. That is a sampling failure, not a negative result.
test.x: The blister must be less than 24 hours old and the biopsy must include the edge with adjacent normal skin. This single detail decides whether the specimen is diagnostic.

test.l: Desmoglein 1 and 3 ELISA, or indirect immunofluorescence
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §6 — titer correlates with disease activity
test.w: To confirm pemphigus, to define the subtype, and thereafter to monitor activity and guide tapering.
test.p: Anti-desmoglein 3 alone indicates mucosal-dominant pemphigus vulgaris; desmoglein 1 and 3 together indicate mucocutaneous disease; desmoglein 1 alone indicates pemphigus foliaceus.
test.n: A negative ELISA in convincing clinical disease should prompt a review of the direct IF rather than abandoning the diagnosis.
test.x: Titers track disease activity, which makes this the most useful monitoring test in pemphigus. Rising titers often precede clinical relapse.

test.l: PCR from a deroofed vesicle base
test.w: Any grouped vesicular eruption, and urgently in suspected eczema herpeticum or disseminated zoster.
test.p: Identifies HSV-1, HSV-2 or VZV specifically. Treat with the appropriate antiviral and dose.
test.n: A negative from a crusted or late lesion does not exclude herpes. Sample a fresh vesicle.
test.x: Deroof the vesicle and swab the base firmly. Swabbing the intact roof is the usual reason for a false negative. Tzanck cytology gives multinucleated giant cells in minutes but cannot separate HSV from VZV — useful when speed matters more than species.

test.l: Tissue transglutaminase IgA with total IgA
test.w: Whenever dermatitis herpetiformis is suspected, and before starting a gluten-free diet.
test.p: Supports gluten-sensitive enteropathy. Refer for gastroenterology assessment and dietitian-supervised gluten withdrawal.
test.n: Selective IgA deficiency produces a false negative, which is why total IgA must be sent with it.
test.x: Serology normalizes on a gluten-free diet, so send it before dietary change or the answer will be uninterpretable.

test.l: Urine porphyrins with plasma fluorescence scan
test.w: Blistering and fragility confined to dorsal hands and sun-exposed sites, particularly with malar hypertrichosis.
test.p: Confirms porphyria cutanea tarda. Then screen for hepatitis C, HIV, iron overload, and review alcohol and estrogen exposure — the skin disease is a marker for all of them.
test.n: A normal porphyrin profile points to pseudoporphyria, which is drug-induced and clinically identical. Review NSAIDs, furosemide, tetracyclines and any recent sun-bed use.
test.x: Bedside screen: urine fluoresces pink-red under a Wood lamp, intensified by dilute hydrochloric acid. Useful, but not a substitute for quantitative porphyrins.

test.w: When linear basement membrane IgG is found but the clinical course does not fit bullous pemphigoid, or when steroids are failing.
test.p: IgG on the dermal (floor) side indicates epidermolysis bullosa acquisita. On the epidermal (roof) side it indicates bullous pemphigoid. This distinction changes the treatment and the prognosis.
test.n: An indeterminate pattern warrants type VII collagen ELISA or Western blot.
test.x: Order this specifically. A standard direct IF report of linear IgG will not distinguish the two and the difference matters, because EBA is characteristically refractory to the doses of prednisone that control pemphigoid.

test.l: Perilesional direct immunofluorescence with BP180 ELISA in pregnancy
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §6 - linear C3 at the basement membrane zone; BP180 autoantibodies detected in over 70%
test.w: Any pruritic urticarial or blistering eruption in the second half of pregnancy or the early postpartum period, particularly when it starts around the umbilicus.
test.p: Linear C3 along the basement membrane zone confirms pemphigoid gestationis. Start prednisone, arrange obstetric surveillance for growth restriction and prematurity, and warn about recurrence in later pregnancies and with estrogen-containing contraception.
test.n: Indirect immunofluorescence is negative in about 80% of genuine cases, so a negative serum study proves nothing. The perilesional direct study and the BP180 ELISA are the tests that count.
test.x: The usual confusion is with polymorphic eruption of pregnancy, which sits in the striae, spares the umbilicus and does not form bullae. If there are true vesicles, take the biopsy.

test.l: Patch testing once the eruption has settled
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §2 - accuracy figures are calibrated estimates
test.w: When the allergen is not obvious, when the dermatitis recurs, or when an occupation or a topical medicament is implicated.
test.p: A positive reaction identifies the allergen. Give a written avoidance list that includes cross-reacting sources.
test.n: A negative standard series does not exclude contact allergy - the relevant allergen may not be on it. Test the person's own products.
test.x: Never patch test with urushiol or plant sap: it sensitizes. Test 2 to 4 weeks after the skin has cleared and off systemic corticosteroids, or the result will be falsely negative.

test.l: Lesional biopsy with direct immunofluorescence to separate EM from SJS/TEN
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §14 - accuracy figures are calibrated estimates
test.w: Target lesions that are blistering, especially with mucosal involvement or any spread onto the trunk.
test.p: Interface dermatitis with apoptotic keratinocytes and a subepidermal split, with negative immunofluorescence, supports erythema multiforme and excludes the autoimmune blistering diseases in the same specimen.
test.n: Histology cannot reliably separate EM major from SJS - that is a clinical judgment based on lesion morphology, distribution and the extent of detachment.
test.x: If there is skin pain, truncal flat atypical targets or a suspect drug, stop the drug and manage as necrolysis while the specimen is processed.

test.l: Salt-split skin immunofluorescence with ANA, anti-dsDNA, complement and urinalysis
test.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin - accuracy figures are calibrated estimates
test.w: Abrupt tense blistering in a young adult, particularly when photodistributed, when lupus is known, or when histology shows neutrophilic papillary microabscesses.
test.p: Immunoreactants on the dermal side of split skin with positive lupus serology confirms bullous systemic lupus. Start dapsone and assess renal involvement.
test.n: Negative lupus serology makes this very unlikely and should redirect you to linear IgA disease, dermatitis herpetiformis or epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, which look identical on routine histology.
test.x: Check G6PD before dapsone. The blistering can be the presenting feature of lupus, so urinalysis and renal function are part of the diagnosis, not an afterthought.

test.l: Immunofluorescence antigen mapping or electron microscopy, with genetic testing
test.s: Fitzpatrick 8e §6 - histopathology determines the level of cleavage, defined further by electron microscopy and immunohistochemical mapping
test.w: Blistering that began at birth or in infancy at trauma sites, and any first adult presentation where inherited disease is suspected.
test.p: The level of the split classifies the disease - intraepidermal simplex, lamina lucida junctional, or sub-lamina densa dystrophic - and that drives prognosis, genetic counseling and cancer surveillance.
test.n: Routine histology alone is not enough. Antigen mapping or electron microscopy localizes the split, and gene testing settles the subtype.
test.x: In an adult presenting for the first time, always send direct immunofluorescence too. Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita mimics dominant dystrophic disease exactly and, unlike it, can be treated.

test.l: Observation off the causative force, with creatine kinase and toxicology after a coma
test.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin - accuracy figures are calibrated estimates
test.w: Blisters confined to a pressure, friction or dependent site, and in anyone found unconscious.
test.p: No new blisters once the force is removed confirms a mechanical cause. After a coma blister, a raised creatine kinase indicates pressure myonecrosis - hydrate, check renal function, and pursue the cause of unconsciousness.
test.n: New blisters at untraumatized sites means this is not mechanical. Take a lesional biopsy and perilesional skin in Michel medium for direct immunofluorescence.
test.x: A coma blister is a clue, not a diagnosis: the question it asks is why the person was unconscious. Do not deroof the blister - the roof is the best dressing available.

flag: Two specimens, not one: lesional skin in formalin for histology, and perilesional normal-appearing skin in Michel medium for direct immunofluorescence. Sampling the blister itself is the commonest reason an autoimmune blistering disease goes unconfirmed.
